Statistics and Financial Data Analysis¶

Sheet 3¶

Q1(a): Construction of Realized Volatility¶

  • Construct log returns between adjacent prices within each recorded calendar date.
  • Calculate daily realized variance and realized volatility, and obtain the last available price on each date.
  • Plot the daily closing exchange rate and realized volatility.
$$ r_{t,i}=\log P_{t,i}-\log P_{t,i-1},\qquad RV_t=\sum_i r_{t,i}^2,\qquad y_t=100\sqrt{RV_t}. $$

We express $y_t$ in daily percentage units; it is not annualised. Missing prices are not filled, cross-date returns are excluded. The file includes Sunday observations. We retain all observed dates, so the 5-day and 22-day averages below refer to consecutive observed days.

In [1]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load GBP/USD five-minute data
df = pd.read_csv("GBPUSD_5min_2013_2022.csv", index_col=0, parse_dates=True)
price = df["GBPUSD"]

# Compute intraday log returns and daily realized volatility
date = price.index.normalize()
returns = np.log(price).groupby(date).diff()
rv = returns.pow(2).groupby(date).sum()

# Construct daily data
daily = pd.DataFrame({
    "Close": price.groupby(date).last(),
    "RV": rv
})
daily["Volatility (%)"] = 100 * np.sqrt(daily["RV"])
y = daily["Volatility (%)"]

# Summary statistics
print(f"Number of daily observations: {len(daily)}")
display(daily[["Close", "Volatility (%)"]].describe().round(4))

Findings:

  • The data produce 3,121 daily volatility observations. Mean and median daily volatility are 0.4796% and 0.4531%, respectively; the largest estimate is 5.2355% on 2016-06-23, using the file's date labels.
  • The exchange rate changes substantially over the sample. Realized volatility alternates between relatively quiet and turbulent periods, with clusters of elevated volatility and occasional large spikes.
  • The series retains 516 Sunday observations. Its observation frequency is therefore usually six dates per week, which matters when interpreting lags and the 5/22-observation HAR averages.

Q1(b): Autoregressive Modelling¶

  • Plot the ACF and PACF to examine persistence and possible autoregressive structure.
In [3]:
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf

max_lag = 22

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.5))

plot_acf(y, lags=36, zero=False, ax=axes[0])
plot_pacf(y, lags=36, zero=False, method="ywm", ax=axes[1])

for ax, title in zip(axes, ["ACF of Daily Volatility", "PACF of Daily Volatility"]):
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Lag (observed days)", ylabel="Correlation")
    ax.set_xticks([1, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36])
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Findings:

  • The ACF is 0.538 at lag 1, 0.537 at lag 6, and 0.443 at lag 12, indicating strong persistence in daily volatility.
  • The PACF shows notable peaks at lags 1, 6, 12, and 18, without a clear low-order cutoff.

We then fit AR($p$) models with an intercept for $p=1,\ldots,22$:

$$ y_t=c+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j y_{t-j}+\varepsilon_t. $$
  • Compare AIC and BIC to select the AR order.
  • Use hold_back=22 to ensure that all candidate models are estimated on the same observations.
In [4]:
from statsmodels.tsa.ar_model import AutoReg

# Fit AR(p) models using the full sample
ar_models = {}
for p in range(1, max_lag + 1):
    ar_models[p] = AutoReg(
        y.to_numpy(), lags=p, trend="c", hold_back=max_lag
    ).fit()

# Compare AIC and BIC
criteria = pd.DataFrame({
    "AIC": {p: model.aic for p, model in ar_models.items()},
    "BIC": {p: model.bic for p, model in ar_models.items()}
})

p_aic = criteria["AIC"].idxmin()
p_bic = criteria["BIC"].idxmin()

print(f"Optimal AR order by AIC: {p_aic}")
print(f"Optimal AR order by BIC: {p_bic}")

# Plot information criteria
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.5))

axes[0].plot(criteria.index, criteria["AIC"], "o-")
axes[0].axvline(p_aic, color="red", linestyle="--", label=f"p = {p_aic}")
axes[0].set(title="AIC", xlabel="AR order", ylabel="AIC")
axes[0].legend()

axes[1].plot(criteria.index, criteria["BIC"], "o-")
axes[1].axvline(p_bic, color="red", linestyle="--", label=f"p = {p_bic}")
axes[1].set(title="BIC", xlabel="AR order", ylabel="BIC")
axes[1].legend()

for ax in axes:
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Optimal AR order by AIC: 22
Optimal AR order by BIC: 19

Findings:

  • AIC selects AR(22), while BIC selects AR(19). BIC favours a slightly simpler model due to its stronger penalty on model complexity.
  • AIC reaches its minimum at the upper boundary of the search range, suggesting that higher AR orders may be worth investigating.
  • Both criteria show noticeable improvements around lags 6, 12, and 18, consistent with the recurring six-observation pattern and persistent volatility dynamics.

Q1(c): Heterogeneous Autoregressive Model¶

We construct three volatility components using different time horizons:

$$ y_t^{(d)}=y_t,\qquad y_t^{(w)}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{j=0}^{4}y_{t-j},\qquad y_t^{(m)}=\frac{1}{22}\sum_{j=0}^{21}y_{t-j}. $$

The HAR model is given by

$$ y_{t+1}=\beta_0+\beta_d y_t^{(d)} +\beta_w y_t^{(w)}+\beta_m y_t^{(m)} +\varepsilon_{t+1}. $$
  • Estimate the HAR model by OLS using the full sample.
  • Compare the estimated coefficients and model complexity with the AR models in Q1(b).
  • Use the same effective estimation period as the AR models for a fair comparison.
In [5]:
import statsmodels.api as sm

# Construct HAR regressors
har_features = pd.DataFrame({
    "Daily": y.shift(1),
    "Mean5": y.rolling(5).mean().shift(1),
    "Mean22": y.rolling(22).mean().shift(1)
})

# Fit HAR using the same observations as the AR models
X_har = sm.add_constant(har_features.iloc[max_lag:])
har = sm.OLS(y.iloc[max_lag:], X_har).fit()

# Display estimated coefficients
display(har.params.to_frame("Coefficient").round(4))

# Compare model complexity and in-sample fit
comparison = []

for label, p in [(f"AR({p_aic}) — AIC", p_aic),
                 (f"AR({p_bic}) — BIC", p_bic)]:
    fit = ar_models[p]
    comparison.append({
        "Model": label,
        "Coefficients": len(fit.params),
        "In-sample RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean(fit.resid**2))
    })

comparison.append({
    "Model": "HAR",
    "Coefficients": len(har.params),
    "In-sample RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean(har.resid**2))
})

display(pd.DataFrame(comparison).set_index("Model").round(4))
Coefficient
const 0.0813
Daily 0.3338
Mean5 0.2319
Mean22 0.2658
Coefficients In-sample RMSE
Model
AR(22) — AIC 23 0.1953
AR(19) — BIC 20 0.1960
HAR 4 0.2240

Findings:

  • The estimated HAR coefficients are 0.3338 (daily), 0.2319 (5-observation) and 0.2658 (22-observation), with an intercept of 0.0813. All three components have positive coefficients, suggesting volatility persistence across different horizons.
  • HAR uses only 4 coefficients, compared with 23 for AR(22) and 20 for AR(19). Its in-sample RMSE is 0.2240, compared with 0.1953 and 0.1960, respectively.
  • HAR provides a more parsimonious representation of volatility dynamics, but its restrictions lead to a higher in-sample prediction error in this application.

The HAR model can be viewed as a restricted AR(22), with lag coefficients

$$ \phi_j= \begin{cases} \beta_d+\beta_w/5+\beta_m/22, & j=1,\\ \beta_w/5+\beta_m/22, & 2\le j\le5,\\ \beta_m/22, & 6\le j\le22. \end{cases} $$

Thus, HAR replaces 22 individual lag coefficients with three coefficients on overlapping averages, reducing model complexity at the cost of flexibility.

In [6]:
# Extract lag coefficients
lags = np.arange(1, max_lag + 1)
ar_weights = ar_models[p_aic].params[1:]

har_weights = np.full(max_lag, har.params["Mean22"] / 22)
har_weights[:5] += har.params["Mean5"] / 5
har_weights[0] += har.params["Daily"]

# Compare AR and HAR lag structures
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(11, 5.5), sharex=True, sharey=True)

axes[0].stem(lags[:p_aic], ar_weights,
             linefmt="C0-", markerfmt="C0o", basefmt=" ")
axes[0].set_title(f"AR({p_aic}): Individually Estimated Lag Coefficients")

axes[1].step(lags, har_weights, where="mid", color="C1", linewidth=2)
axes[1].scatter(lags, har_weights, color="C1", s=15, zorder=3)
axes[1].set_title("HAR: Restricted Lag Coefficients")

for ax in axes:
    ax.axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_ylabel("Coefficient")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2, linestyle="--")

axes[1].set_xlabel("Lag (observed days)")
axes[1].set_xticks([1, 5, 6, 12, 18, 22])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Findings:

  • The AR(22) coefficients at lags 6, 12, and 18 are approximately 0.243, 0.180, and 0.229, respectively. In contrast, HAR assigns a common coefficient of approximately 0.012 to all lags from 6 to 22.
  • The HAR model cannot capture these individual lag peaks due to its restricted coefficient structure. This helps explain its weaker in-sample fit compared with AR(22).

Q1(d): Out-of-Sample Forecasting¶

  • Split the data chronologically into 80% training and 20% test observations.
  • Re-select the AR orders using AIC and BIC, and re-estimate the AR and HAR models using only the training sample.
  • Generate one-step-ahead forecasts using the estimated parameters and the latest observed volatility.
  • Compare the forecasts using RMSE and MAE, including the persistence benchmark $\widehat y_t=y_{t-1}$.

For each test observation, the forecast uses actual volatility values available up to the previous date. Model parameters remain fixed throughout the test period.

In [7]:
# Split data into training and test samples
n_train = int(0.8 * len(y))
train, test = y.iloc[:n_train], y.iloc[n_train:]

# Re-select AR orders using training data
ar_train = {
    p: AutoReg(train.to_numpy(), lags=p, trend="c",
               hold_back=max_lag).fit()
    for p in range(1, max_lag + 1)
}

p_aic_train = min(ar_train, key=lambda p: ar_train[p].aic)
p_bic_train = min(ar_train, key=lambda p: ar_train[p].bic)

# Re-estimate HAR using training data
X_har_train = sm.add_constant(har_features.iloc[max_lag:n_train])
har_train = sm.OLS(train.iloc[max_lag:], X_har_train).fit()

# Construct one-step-ahead forecasts
lagged_y = pd.DataFrame({
    f"lag{j}": y.shift(j) for j in range(1, max_lag + 1)
})
forecasts = pd.DataFrame(index=test.index)

for label, p in [(f"AR({p_aic_train}) - AIC", p_aic_train),
                 (f"AR({p_bic_train}) - BIC", p_bic_train)]:
    X_test = sm.add_constant(
        lagged_y.loc[test.index].iloc[:, :p], has_constant="add"
    )
    forecasts[label] = X_test.to_numpy() @ ar_train[p].params

forecasts["HAR"] = har_train.predict(
    sm.add_constant(har_features.loc[test.index])
)
forecasts["Persistence"] = y.shift(1).loc[test.index]

# Evaluate forecast accuracy
errors = forecasts.sub(test, axis=0)
scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "RMSE": np.sqrt(errors.pow(2).mean()),
    "MAE": errors.abs().mean()
})
display(scores.round(4))

print(f"Training: {len(train)} observations; Test: {len(test)} observations")
print(f"Selected AR orders: AIC = {p_aic_train}, BIC = {p_bic_train}")
RMSE MAE
AR(22) - AIC 0.1899 0.1054
AR(19) - BIC 0.1904 0.1058
HAR 0.2149 0.1354
Persistence 0.2459 0.1719 
Training: 2496 observations; Test: 625 observations
Selected AR orders: AIC = 22, BIC = 19
In [8]:
# Plot one-step-ahead forecasts
model_names = list(forecasts.columns[:3])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(12, 7), sharex=True, sharey=True)

for ax, model in zip(axes, model_names):
    ax.plot(test.index, test, color="lightgray", lw=1,
            label="Observed")
    ax.plot(test.index, forecasts[model], lw=1.3,
            label="Forecast")

    ax.set_title(model, loc="left", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("Volatility (%)")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)

axes[-1].set_xlabel("Date")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Findings:

  • AR(22) achieves the lowest out-of-sample RMSE (0.1899) and MAE (0.1054), closely followed by AR(19) (0.1904 and 0.1058). The difference is marginal, suggesting little additional predictive benefit from the more complex model.
  • HAR has a higher RMSE (0.2149) and MAE (0.1354), but still outperforms the persistence benchmark. The AR models benefit from their flexibility in capturing individual lag effects, particularly the recurring six-observation pattern.
  • All models capture the general level of volatility but struggle to predict extreme movements. For example, observed volatility reaches 3.394% on 2022-09-25, substantially exceeding all three forecasts.

Conclusion: The higher-order AR models provide better out-of-sample forecasts in this application, while HAR offers a simpler alternative with fewer parameters.

Q2(b): Stationarity and Unit Root Tests¶

  • Examine the time-series behaviour of daily trading volume and its first difference.
  • Apply the Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test to both series.
  • Determine whether differencing is necessary before fitting an ARIMA model.

The ADF test has the null hypothesis that the series contains a unit root.

In [10]:
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

# Original volume and first differences (in millions)
v = volume / 1e6
dv = v.diff().dropna()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(11, 6), sharex=True)

axes[0].plot(v.index, v, lw=0.9, alpha=0.6, label="Daily volume")
axes[0].plot(v.rolling(20).mean(), lw=2, label="20-day moving average")
axes[0].set(title="GOOG Daily Trading Volume", ylabel="Shares (millions)")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)

axes[1].plot(dv.index, dv, lw=0.9)
axes[1].axhline(0, color="gray", ls="--", lw=0.8)
axes[1].set(title="First Difference of Trading Volume",
            xlabel="Date", ylabel="Change (millions)")

for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.15)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


# ADF unit root tests
for name, series in [("Original", v), ("First difference", dv)]:
    result = adfuller(series, autolag="AIC", result_object=False)
    print(f"{name}: ADF = {result[0]:.4f}, p-value = {result[1]:.4g}")

Original: ADF = -3.2897, p-value = 0.01535
First difference: ADF = -14.7833, p-value = 2.228e-27

Findings:

  • Daily trading volume exhibits substantial fluctuations and occasional extreme spikes. The first-differenced series fluctuates around zero.
  • The ADF test rejects the unit-root hypothesis for both the original series (ADF = -3.2897, p = 0.0153) and its first difference (ADF = -14.7833, p < 0.001).
  • Since the original series already rejects the unit-root hypothesis, differencing is not necessary on this evidence. We therefore consider ARMA models, corresponding to ARIMA models with $d=0$.

Q2(c): ARIMA Model Selection and Diagnostics¶

  • Examine the ACF and PACF of daily trading volume.
  • Fit ARIMA$(p,0,q)$ models for $p,q=0,\ldots,3$, and select the preferred model using AIC and BIC.
  • Examine the residuals of the selected model using the residual ACF and Ljung–Box test.

Since the ADF test rejects the unit-root hypothesis, we set $d=0$ and consider ARMA models.

In [11]:
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
import warnings
from statsmodels.tools.sm_exceptions import EstimationWarning, ConvergenceWarning

# ARMA model selection
models = {}
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", EstimationWarning)
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", ConvergenceWarning)

    for p in range(4):
        for q in range(4):
            models[(p, q)] = ARIMA(
                v.to_numpy(), order=(p, 0, q)
            ).fit()

criteria = pd.DataFrame({
    "AIC": {order: fit.aic for order, fit in models.items()},
    "BIC": {order: fit.bic for order, fit in models.items()}
})

best_aic = criteria["AIC"].idxmin()
best_bic = criteria["BIC"].idxmin()

print(f"Best model by AIC: ARMA{best_aic}")
print(f"Best model by BIC: ARMA{best_bic}")
display(criteria.sort_values("AIC").head(6).round(2))

Best model by AIC: ARMA(3, 2)
Best model by BIC: ARMA(2, 2)
AIC BIC
3 2 18357.68 18396.79
2 2 18362.90 18396.42
3 3 18366.75 18411.44
1 18369.03 18402.56
1 3 18373.94 18407.46
2 18396.12 18424.05

Findings:

  • The ACF shows positive serial dependence, while the PACF has a prominent spike at lag 1, suggesting an autoregressive structure.
  • AIC selects ARMA(3,2), while BIC selects ARMA(2,2), among the candidate models. The AIC-selected model has AIC = 18357.68 and BIC = 18396.79.
  • The residual ACF and Ljung–Box test assess whether significant serial correlation remains after fitting the model. Small Ljung–Box p-values indicate remaining autocorrelation and suggest that the selected model does not fully capture the dependence structure.

Q3(a): Data Preparation and Exploratory Analysis¶

We consider the UK labour productivity index (output per worker, seasonally adjusted) from 1997Q1 to 2025Q4, obtained from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

  • Load the quarterly productivity index from mfp(2).csv.
  • Compute quarterly log growth rates:
$$ g_t=100\left(\log P_t-\log P_{t-1}\right), $$

where $P_t$ denotes the productivity index.

  • Plot the productivity index and its quarterly growth rates to examine their time-series behaviour.
In [13]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates

# Load quarterly productivity data
data = pd.read_csv("mfp.csv")
data = data[data["Title"].str.match(r"^\d{4} Q[1-4]$")].copy()
data.index = pd.PeriodIndex(data["Title"].str.replace(" ", ""), freq="Q")

productivity = pd.to_numeric(
    data.loc["1997Q1":"2025Q4"].iloc[:, 1]
).rename("Productivity")

# Compute quarterly log growth rates
growth = (100 * np.log(productivity).diff()).dropna()

print(f"Quarterly observations: {len(productivity)}")
display(productivity.describe().round(3))

# Figure settings
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "DejaVu Serif",
    "font.size": 9,
    "axes.titlesize": 10,
    "axes.labelsize": 9,
    "xtick.labelsize": 8,
    "ytick.labelsize": 8,
    "figure.dpi": 150
})

blue = "#32659A"
gray = "#777777"
dates = productivity.index.to_timestamp()
growth_dates = growth.index.to_timestamp()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    2, 1, figsize=(9.5, 5.8), sharex=True,
    gridspec_kw={"hspace": 0.27}
)

# (a) Productivity index
axes[0].plot(dates, productivity, color=blue, lw=1.7)
axes[0].set_title("(a) UK labour productivity index", loc="left", pad=9)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Index (2024 = 100)")

# (b) Quarterly growth
lower, upper = -3, 3
clipped = growth.clip(lower, upper)

axes[1].bar(
    growth_dates, clipped, width=65,
    color=np.where(growth >= 0, blue, gray),
    alpha=0.85, linewidth=0
)
axes[1].axhline(0, color="0.45", lw=0.8, ls="--")
axes[1].set_ylim(-3.2, 3.2)
axes[1].set_title("(b) Quarterly log productivity growth", loc="left", pad=9)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Growth (%)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Year")

# Mark values outside the displayed range
high = growth > upper
low = growth < lower

axes[1].scatter(
    growth_dates[high], np.full(high.sum(), upper),
    marker="^", s=28, color=blue, zorder=5
)
axes[1].scatter(
    growth_dates[low], np.full(low.sum(), lower),
    marker="v", s=28, color=gray, zorder=5
)

# Shared styling
for ax in axes:
    for year in [2008, 2020]:
        ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp(f"{year}-01-01"),
                   color="0.55", lw=0.8, ls=":", zorder=1)

    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines[["left", "bottom"]].set_color("0.65")
    ax.tick_params(length=3, width=0.6, color="0.5")
    ax.grid(axis="y", color="0.85", alpha=0.4, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.margins(x=0.01)

axes[1].xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator(4))
axes[1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.10, right=0.985, top=0.94, bottom=0.12)
plt.show()

Findings:

  • The UK labour productivity index increased substantially between 1997 and 2007, followed by much slower growth after the 2008 financial crisis. Productivity remained relatively stagnant over much of the subsequent period.
  • Quarterly productivity growth fluctuates around a relatively low positive level, with occasional negative quarters. The fluctuations become particularly pronounced during the COVID-19 pandemic.
  • The pandemic period exhibits extreme movements, including a sharp decline of approximately 20.5% followed by a rebound exceeding 16%. These observations suggest that structural disruptions and outliers may affect subsequent time-series modelling.

Overall, the productivity index exhibits a long-term trend, while quarterly growth rates appear more stable apart from major economic disruptions.

Q3(b): Comparing Productivity Growth Across Periods¶

  • Compare quarterly productivity growth before and after the 2008 financial crisis, using 1997–2007 and 2008–2018.
  • Compare the five years before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, using 2015–2019 and 2021–2025, excluding 2020.
  • Report the mean growth rates and test whether the differences are statistically significant.

For each comparison, consider the difference in mean quarterly growth rates:

$$ \Delta=\mu_{\mathrm{post}}-\mu_{\mathrm{pre}}. $$

Use a two-sample Welch test and a regression with HAC standard errors to account for possible serial correlation and heteroskedasticity.

In [14]:
import statsmodels.api as sm
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

# Define comparison periods
periods = [
    ("1997–2007", "1997Q2", "2007Q4"),
    ("2008–2018", "2008Q1", "2018Q4"),
    ("2015–2019", "2015Q1", "2019Q4"),
    ("2021–2025", "2021Q1", "2025Q4")
]

samples = {}
rows = []

for label, start, end in periods:
    x = growth.loc[start:end]
    samples[label] = x

    fit = sm.OLS(x.to_numpy(), np.ones((len(x), 1))).fit(
        cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4}
    )
    rows.append({
        "Period": label,
        "N": len(x),
        "Mean (%)": x.mean(),
        "Std. Dev.": x.std(),
        "HAC SE": fit.bse[0]
    })

summary = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Period")
display(summary.round(4))

# Test differences in mean growth
comparisons = [
    ("Financial crisis", "1997–2007", "2008–2018"),
    ("COVID-19", "2015–2019", "2021–2025")
]

results = []

for event, pre, post in comparisons:
    x, z = samples[pre], samples[post]
    values = np.r_[x.values, z.values]
    indicator = np.r_[np.zeros(len(x)), np.ones(len(z))]

    fit = sm.OLS(values, sm.add_constant(indicator)).fit(
        cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4}
    )

    results.append({
        "Comparison": event,
        "Mean difference": z.mean() - x.mean(),
        "Welch p-value": ttest_ind(z, x, equal_var=False).pvalue,
        "HAC p-value": fit.pvalues[1]
    })

display(pd.DataFrame(results).set_index("Comparison").round(4))

# Plot mean growth with HAC confidence intervals
blue, gray = "#32659A", "#777777"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 3.2), dpi=150)

for ax, (event, pre, post), title in zip(
    axes, comparisons,
    ["(a) Financial crisis", "(b) COVID-19"]
):
    sub = summary.loc[[pre, post]]
    means = sub["Mean (%)"].values
    errors = 1.96 * sub["HAC SE"].values

    ax.errorbar(
        [0, 1], means, yerr=errors, fmt="o",
        color=blue, ecolor="0.45", markersize=7,
        capsize=5, elinewidth=1.2
    )
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.55", lw=0.8, ls="--")
    ax.set_xticks([0, 1], [pre, post])
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", pad=9)
    ax.set_ylabel("Mean quarterly growth (%)")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.4, 1.4)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(axis="y", color="0.85", alpha=0.4, lw=0.6)

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.09, right=0.98,
                    bottom=0.18, top=0.85, wspace=0.28)
plt.show()

Findings:

  • Financial crisis: Mean quarterly productivity growth declined from 0.432% in 1997–2007 to 0.139% in 2008–2018. The difference is statistically significant under both the Welch test ($p=0.0078$) and the HAC test ($p=0.0484$).
  • COVID-19: Mean growth increased from 0.208% in 2015–2019 to 0.388% in 2021–2025, but the difference is not statistically significant (HAC $p=0.5490$).
  • The post-pandemic sample exhibits much greater variability, partly reflecting the sharp recovery in 2021. Consequently, the higher average growth rate should not be interpreted as evidence of a sustained improvement.

Conclusion: UK labour productivity experienced a statistically significant slowdown after the 2008 financial crisis, whereas the five-year comparison around COVID-19 provides no significant evidence of a change in average quarterly growth.
